title: 1.1.23 Unit 1.1 Quiz
description: Ten multiple-choice questions on the four phases, umbrella activities, actions and task sets, the four Ps, and prescriptive models. Checked instantly.

questions.question: What is a process model?
options: A plan for what happens when in a software project
The programming language a team has chosen
A drawing of what the finished app will look like
The person who decides what gets built
questions.explanation: A process model gives the project its shape: it says what happens when. Teams do not build in random order.

questions.question: What are the four framework activities, in order?
options: Design, development, testing, deployment
Inception, elaboration, construction, deployment
Planning, drawing, typing, shipping
Problem, project, people, product
questions.explanation: Inception, elaboration, construction, deployment. Every process model uses these same four: what changes is how much work each one gets.

questions.question: Which phase does the line `console.log("Hello, " + name + "!")` belong to?
options: Inception: it is the goal of the app
Elaboration: it is the design
Construction: it is the actual code being written
Deployment: it is what the user sees
questions.explanation: Construction is where the software is coded and built from the design. Worth noticing: that line is one phase out of four: teams tend to over-weight construction.

questions.question: Which phase is where requirements are analyzed and the architecture is designed?
options: Inception
Elaboration
Construction
Deployment
questions.explanation: Elaboration. Inception sets the goals and scope; elaboration turns them into requirements and a design.

questions.question: What makes an umbrella activity different from a phase?
options: It runs alongside every phase instead of sitting inside one
It happens only at the very end of a project
It is work only managers do
It is a phase that can be skipped on small projects
questions.explanation: An umbrella activity never starts and ends: it runs the whole project. The kitchen analogy: the four phases are cooking the meal, umbrella activities are the cleanup that keeps the kitchen usable throughout.

questions.question: Which of these is an umbrella activity?
options: Construction
Risk management
Inception
Writing the greeting function
questions.explanation: Risk management is one of the six: training/communication, risk management, configuration management, quality management, architecture management, security management.

questions.question: What is a software engineering action?
options: A single keystroke or line of code
Another word for a phase
A named job inside a phase, such as "define the requirements"
A meeting held at the start of a project
questions.explanation: An action answers what job gets done inside a phase. It is not the whole phase and not a single keystroke: "define the requirements" lives inside inception.

questions.question: What is a task set?
options: All the tasks required to accomplish one software engineering action
The list of every phase in the project
The set of tools a team has installed
A single task that finishes a whole phase
questions.explanation: One action = one task set. Each task in the set produces a real work product, and that work product is checked before moving on.

questions.question: What are the four Ps?
options: Plan, program, publish, patch
Problem, project, people, product
Process, prototype, production, polish
Purpose, priority, progress, proof
questions.explanation: Problem, project, people, product. They are the reason two teams following the same four phases still work very differently.

questions.question: Why is a prescriptive process model a poor fit for a project whose requirements change every week?
options: It only works for very large teams
It requires a programming language the team may not know
It advocates an orderly, prescribed sequence, and that rigidity cannot bend when requirements keep moving
It has no testing phase
questions.explanation: Prescriptive means it hands you a prescribed order to follow. That is a strength when requirements are stable and a weakness when they are not: the strict-recipe problem.
